I am 51 years old and have been farming these lands in Quzhou since I was a young man. I never went to school, but I know these fields. Every year, I grow winter wheat and summer maize on the same plots — it is the rotation my father taught me, and it feeds my family.

My wheat went into the ground last October. I have about 8 mu of good flat land. Right now the wheat is greening up, and the first thing I will do when the soil warms is apply top-dressing urea — about 45 kg per mu of nitrogen. I will irrigate three or four times before harvest: once in spring to help the tillering, once at jointing, and again at filling if the sky stays dry. I always do rotary tillage before sowing wheat, but that was done last autumn. For pests and weeds, I spray herbicide once and insecticide twice — the aphids and powdery mildew always come if you are not careful. I use improved wheat seed, sowing about 30 jin per mu. If the weather is fair, I expect around 1,000 jin of grain per mu.

After I harvest the wheat in early June, I will immediately plant summer maize on the same 8 mu. I do not till the soil again for maize — I plant directly into the wheat stubble. It saves time, saves fuel, and the straw helps keep moisture. I use hybrid maize seed, about 1 kg per mu. Maize does not need as much nitrogen as wheat, but I give it about 15 kg per mu of nitrogen from compound fertilizer at sowing, plus a little phosphorus and potassium. I irrigate twice for maize, usually once right after sowing and once at the big-ear stage. I spray herbicide once and insecticide twice to control weeds and the corn borer. With luck, the maize will yield about 1,100 jin per mu.

I do not try strange new crops. Wheat and maize are safe. The dealers at the market buy them every year. That is my plan.
